Images of maps from (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) to (ℂn,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0)

Helge Møller Pedersen Address: Departamento de Matemática
Universidade Federal do Ceará
Campus do Pici, Bloco 914
CEP 60455-760, Fortaleza, CE
Brazil Email address: helge@mat.ufc.br
Abstract.

Let F:(ℂ2,0)→(ℂn,0)F\colon(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) be the germ of a finite map and (X,0)(X,0) be its image. We will in this article using the topology of the link show that (X,0)(X,0) has to be a quotient singularity if it is normal. We will also discuss the case when the image is not normal. Finally we describe the possible topological types, including a discussion of the groups and examples of how to construct a map to a given topology.

1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
14B05, 32S05, 32S25, 32S50, 57K30, 57M10, 57M60

1. Introduction

The study of germs of holomorphic maps f:(ℂm,0)→(ℂn,0)f\colon(\mathbbm{C}^{m},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) is a very active field of study. The case when m=2m=2 is of particular interest. Especially the case of finite determined germs have been studied a lot. On of the great achievements of singularity theorem is the classification of finitely determined map germs f:(ℂ2,0)→(ℂ3,0)f\colon(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{3},0) by Mond [Mon85]. Their images have also seen great interest. It has, for example, been discovered that the relationship between the image Milnor number and the 𝒜\mathscr{A}-codimension looks a lot like the relationship between Milnor and Tjurina numbers for hypersurfaces [dJvS91, dJvS91, Mon95]. For a pretty recent overview of the theory see [MNnB20].

Now finitely determined maps are finite and generically one to one, so in light of this Guillermo Peñafort Sanchis asked the following question: “Which germs of surface singularities in ℂ3\mathbbm{C}^{3} can be the image of a germ of a finite maps from ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2}?” during the conference: 60LB Geometry and Singularities – 60th anniversary of Lev Birbrair. It is clear that if one wants to try to push Mond’s classification to a more general groups of map germs that are finite and generically kk to one, then one would need an answer to this question.

An obvious example of the image of a finite holomorphic map is the AnA_{n} singularity given by x​y=znxy=z^{n}, which is clearly the image of (sn,tn,s​t)(s^{n},t^{n},st). Notice that AnA_{n} is a cyclic quotient singularity, that is the quotient of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) by ℤ/n​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/n\mathbbm{Z} acting by rotation. In general if (X,0)(X,0) is the quotient of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) by an algebraic group then it follows that the quotient map will have (X,0)(X,0) as its image, though it will not necessarily be a singularity in ℂ3\mathbbm{C}^{3} but may instead be in ℂn\mathbbm{C}^{n} for some nn.

Javier Fernández de Bobadilla gave us the hint that one should look at the restriction of the map to a preimage of the link of (X,0)(X,0). Which is what we will do in this article.

The study of 3-manifolds, particularly those that arise as links of complex surface singularities, is well-established. By using the knowledge we have of 3-manifolds, we prove the following.

Theorem 1.1.

Let (X,0)⊂(ℂn,0)(X,0)\subset(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) be the germ of a normal surface singularity. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (I)

    (X,0)(X,0) is the image of a finite holomorphic map F:(ℂ2,0)→(ℂn,0)F:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0).

  2. (II)

    (X,0)(X,0) is a quotient of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) by a finite subgroup of U⁡(2)U(2) acting linearly.

  3. (III)

    π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is finite where LL is the link of (X,0)(X,0).

The equivalence between (II) and (III) is a classical result, one direction follows by a Theorem of Prill [Pri67], the other direction is even simpler to observe. It follows from this that the group acting in (II) is π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L), and we will list all the possible groups and the corresponding topologies of (X,0)(X,0) and its link. They all turn out to be taut and rational singularities. Specifically in the case the image is a hypersurface, it is one of the simple AkA_{k}, DkD_{k}, E6E_{6}, E7E_{7} and E8E_{8} singularities. We will construct maps that realize the simple singularities as their images, and give a way to construct maps for other groups with some examples.

The assumption of 1.1 that (X,0)(X,0) is normal is a very common assumption when spaces are considered, since the normalization does not change the topological type of an isolated singularity. For maps it turns out that one cannot in general make the assumption that the image is normal, any finitely determined map that is not an embedding do in fact have image the is not normal. Listing all the non normal singularities, that are the images of finite holomorphic maps, seem out of reach for the moment. But we provide the following algorithm for determining when a given surface singularity is the image of a finite holomorphic map:

Algorithm 1.2.

Let (X,0)(X,0) be the germ of an irreducible complex surface singularity. Then the following steps will determine if it is the image of a finite map:

  1. (1)

    Determine the normalization n:(X~,0)→(X,0)n:(\widetilde{X},0)\to(X,0).

  2. (2)

    Calculate the fundamental group of the link L~\widetilde{L} of the (X~,0)(\widetilde{X},0).

Then (X,0)(X,0) is the image of a finite map if and only if π1​(L~)\pi_{1}(\widetilde{L}) is finite.

In the case the answer is positive then one obtains a map F:(ℂ2,0)→(X,0)F:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(X,0) as n∘qn\circ q where q:(ℂ2,0)→(X~,0)q:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\widetilde{X},0) is a map realizing (X~,0)(\widetilde{X},0) as the quotient of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) under the action of π1​(L~)\pi_{1}(\widetilde{L}).

In step (2) one can instead of calculating π1​(L~)\pi_{1}(\widetilde{L}) determine if (X~,0)(\widetilde{X},0) is one of the singularities we describe in section 5, for example by determining the topology of L~\widetilde{L} by obtaining its plumbing graph as the dual graph of a good resolution. Then qq is given by the maps we discus in section 5 up to a change of coordinates.

We start by reviewing the 3-manifold topology needed to prove Theorem 1.1 in section 2, and the proof is then done in Section 3. In Section 4 we will consider the case of non normal image and give the proof of 1.2. In Section 5 we will give a detailed description of the topologies that can appear as the images of finite map germs including which groups have them as quotients. We will also construct map realizing all the simple singularities as images of finite map germs and, show how to construct the maps in the general case with some examples.

2. Review of the topology of 3-manifolds

In this section we are going to give a short review with reference of the three dimensional topology that is used in the proof of the main theorem. We assume that all manifolds are orientable, compact and without boundaries and will therefore only state the results in these cases. This assumption will be satisfied by the manifolds we are concerned with in later sections, since they are boundaries of complex manifolds.

Definition 2.1.

A three dimensional manifold MM is called irreducible if every embedded two sphere in MM bounds a ball.

It is Theorem 1 of Neumann in [Neu81] that the link of a normal complex surface singularity is an irreducible 3 manifold.

Next we have the Sphere Theorem by Papakyriakopoulos

Theorem 2.2.

If MM is a 3-manifold and NN a π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M)-invariant subgroup of π2​(M)\pi_{2}(M) with π2​(M)∖N≠∅\pi_{2}(M)\setminus N\neq\emptyset, then there is an embedding g:S2→Mg\colon S^{2}\to M such that the class of gg in π2​(M)\pi_{2}(M) is not in NN.

(For more on this Theorem see for example Chapter 4 of [Hem76]) Noticed that the trivial subgroup of π2​(M)\pi_{2}(M) is π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M)-invariant. So if π2​(M)\pi_{2}(M) is not trivial, then the theorem stats that there is an embedded S2S^{2} representing a non trivial element of π2​(M)\pi_{2}(M). But if MM is irreducible then any embedded S2S^{2} bounds a ball, and hence represents the trivial element of Π2​(M)\Pi_{2}(M). So we can conclude.

Corollary 2.3.

If MM is an irreducible 3-manifold, then π2​(M)\pi_{2}(M) is trivial.

Next we need some results about the types of irreducible 3-manifolds that can be the link of a complex surface singularity.

Definition 2.4.

A Seifert fibration is a triple (M,f,Σ)(M,f,\Sigma) where MM is a 3-manifold, Σ\Sigma is a surface and f:M→Σf\colon M\to\Sigma is smooth map with the following properties:

  1. (1)

    For every x∈Σx\in\Sigma there is a disc neighbourhood DD of xx such that f−1​(D)≅S1×Df^{-1}(D)\cong S^{1}\times D.

  2. (2)

    If (t1,r​t2)(t_{1},rt_{2}) are polar coordinates on f−1​(D)≅S1×Df^{-1}(D)\cong S^{1}\times D then thre exist p,q∈ℤp,q\in\mathbbm{Z} depending on xx with gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1 and p≠0p\neq 0 such that f⁡(t1,r​t2)=r​t1q​t3pf(t_{1},rt_{2})=rt_{1}^{q}t_{3}^{p}.

A 3-manifold that posses a Siefert fibration is called a Seifert fibred 3-manifold.

Examples of Seifert fibred manifolds are S3S^{3}, with the hop-fibration, circle-bundles in general, lens spaces whit a Seifert fibration coming as a quotient of the Hopf-fibration of S3S^{3}.

The definition of Seifert fibred manifolds does not assume that Σ\Sigma is an oriented surface, but in our case Σ\Sigma will correspond to complex curves and therefore has to be oriented. So we will assume the Σ\Sigma is oriented. Except for the lens spaces (here we count S3S^{3} and S1×S2S^{1}\times S^{2}) then any homeomorphism of a Seifert fibred manifold preserves the Seifert fibration. (Here again is used that the base surface is oriented, if not there are a few extra exceptions)

A fibre of the Siefert fibration is called singular if the value of pp not equal to +1+1. Since MM is compact then the number of singular fibres is finite. It follows that any Siefert fibration can then be encoded by the Seifert data which can be put in a normal form as (g,(1,b),(p1,q1),…,(p1,qn))\bigl(g,(1,b),(p_{1},q_{1}),\dots,(p_{1},q_{n})\bigr). Here gg is the genus of Σ\Sigma, (p1,qi)(p_{1},q_{i}) are invariants of the singular fibres with gcd⁡(p1,qi)=1\gcd(p_{1},q_{i})=1 and 1≤qi<pi1\leq q_{i}<p_{i} (pip_{i} is the same as in the definition, but qiq_{i} is different) and bb is the euler number of the fibration of the compliment of the singular fibres. For a lens space L⁡(p,q)L(p,q) we simple associate the Seifert invariants (0,(1,0),(p,q))\bigl(0,(1,0),(p,q)\bigr). There are different conventions of how to present the Seifert invariants, and we will follow the one from [Neu07], see also [JN83] for a detailed construction but be aware they use to oposite convention for the Seifert invariants. We will use the Seifert invariants in section 5 when we want to see the precise topology of the images of finite holomorphic maps.

Definition 2.5.

Let MM be a 3-manifold, then an embedded surface Σ∈M\Sigma\in M is called compressible, if on of the following holds:

  1. (1)

    Σ\Sigma is s sphere and it bounds a ball.

  2. (2)

    There is an immersed disc D⊂MD\subset M such that D∩Σ=∂DD\cap\Sigma=\partial D and ∂D\partial D is not contractible in Σ\Sigma.

Σ\Sigma is called incompressible if it is not compressible.

Incompressible surfaces have the following property which will be used later, for proof of this see for example [Hem76] Corollary 6.2.

Proposition 2.6.

Let Σ⊂M\Sigma\subset M be an oriented incompressible surface, then ker⁡(π1​(Σ)↦π1​(M))\ker(\pi_{1}(\Sigma)\mapsto\pi_{1}(M)) is trivial.

The main reason for introducing incompressible surface is the following decomposition theorem for irreducible three manifolds by Jaco and Salen [JS79] and independetly Johannson [Joh79].

Theorem 2.7 (JSJ-Decomposition).

Let MM be a irreducible 3-manifold, then there exist a maximal sets of pairwise non isotopic incompressible tori T1,…​TkT_{1},\dots T_{k}, which is unique up to isotopy and reordering, such that M∖(T1∪⋯∪Tk)M\setminus\bigl(T_{1}\cup\dots\cup T_{k}\bigr) is a collection of Seifert fibred (with solid tori consisting of fibres removed) or atoroidal manifolds.

A manifold MM is atoriodal if every embedded tori either bounds a solid tori or is isotopic to a boundary component of MM.

Definition 2.8.

An irreducible 3-manifold is called a graph manifold if every piece of its JSJ-decomposition is Seifert fibred.

There is a class of 3-manifolds called plumbed 3-manifolds which by results of Waldhausen is the same as graph manifolds [Wal67]. It follows from classical result in resolution of surface singularities [DV44] that the link of a normal surface singularity is a plumbed 3-manifold given by the dual resolution graph, and hence a graph manifold. We will describe the plumbing construction in more detail in section 5, where we use it to study the links of the images of finite maps by giving their dual resolution graphs.

3. Maps from S3S^{3}

To prove the main Theorem we want to reduce to topological arguments, and we do that by looking at the map induced by f:(ℂ2,0)→(ℂ,0)f\colon(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C},0) between the “links” of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) and (Im⁡f,0)(\operatorname{Im}f,0). So one needs that ff in fact induces such maps. This seems to be the case in general for finite maps, not just for the case the domain is ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2}. The result we could in the literature is part (i)(i) of Theorem 3 by Fukuda in the article [Fuk82], which shows it under a generality condition on ff, which we are not sure contains all finite map germs. He also does not state to prove it in the case of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0), but that is just because the Poincare Conjecture was not proven in that dimension when he wrote his article.

We will give a proof that works for all finite maps, but our proof only works in the case of maps from (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) since it will rely on 3-dimensional topology. We start with a very general lemma which is probably know to experts and seem to be implicitly used in Fukuda’s result.

Lemma 3.1.

Let LL be a finite nn-dimensional CW-complex and X:=L×[0,1]/(x,0)∼(y,0)X:=L\times[0,1]/(x,0)\sim(y,0) be the cone over LL. Suppose that X∖LX\setminus L is and topological manifold, then LL is a homotopy sphere. In particularly if LL is a manifold then it is homeomorphic to SnS^{n}.

Proof.

Let x∗∈Xx^{*}\in X be the cone point and BB a open ball neighbourhood of x∗x^{*} in XX. Let L∗:=X∖{x∗}L^{*}:=X\setminus\{x^{*}\} and B∗:=B∖{x∗}B^{*}:=B\setminus\{x^{*}\}. Then X=L∗∪BX=L^{*}\cup B and L∗∩B=B∗L^{*}\cap B=B^{*}. Now XX nad BB are contractible so it follows from the Meyer-Vietoris sequence that the inclusion of B∗B^{*} in L∗L^{*} induces the isomorphism Hi​(L∗)≅Hi​(B∗)H_{i}(L^{*})\cong H_{i}(B^{*}) for all ii. But L∗L^{*} is homotopic to LL and B∗B^{*} is homotopic to SnS^{n}. So Hi​(L)≅Hi​(Sn)H_{i}(L)\cong H_{i}(S^{n}) for all ii. Since B∗B^{*} is simply connected it follows from Seifert-Van Kampen’s Theorem that π1​(X)≅π1​(B)∗π1​(L∗)≅π1​(L)\pi_{1}(X)\cong\pi_{1}(B)*\pi_{1}(L^{*})\cong\pi_{1}(L), here we use n>2n>2 but it is easy to modify the argument in the case n=2n=2. But XX is contractible so π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is trivial. Since LL is a finite CW-complex it follows form Whitehead’s Theorem that it is homotopic to SnS^{n}. Then if LL is a manifold it is homeomorphic to SnS^{n} by the Poincare Hypothesis. ∎

In our case we do not actually need the Poincare Conjecture to draw the last conclusion. As we will see later, graph manifolds with trivial fundamental group being homeomorphic to S3S^{3} was know long before the proof of the Poincare Conjecture in three dimensions by Perelman.

Lemma 3.2.

Let F:(ℂ2,0)→(ℂn,0)F:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) be a germ of a finite holomorphic map and Lε=Sε2​n−1∩Im⁡FL_{\varepsilon}=S^{2n-1}_{\varepsilon}\cap\operatorname{Im}F be the link of (Im⁡F,0)(\operatorname{Im}F,0). Then there exist an ε0\varepsilon_{0} such that for 0<ε<ε00<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0} the preimage S~:=F−1​(Lε)\widetilde{S}:=F^{-1}(L_{\varepsilon}) is homeomorphic to S3S^{3}.

Proof.

We chose a proper representative of the FF, which we denote by ff, such that f−1​(0)={0}f^{-1}(0)=\{0\}. Which is possible since FF is the germ of a finite map. Then we can choose Bε0⊂ℂnB_{\varepsilon_{0}}\subset\mathbbm{C}^{n} such that the set of critical values Σ⁡(f)\Sigma(f) of ff is a finite union of irreducible complex curves C1C_{1}, …CkC_{k} in Xε0:=Bε0∩Im⁡fX_{\varepsilon_{0}}:=B_{\varepsilon_{0}}\cap\operatorname{Im}f. Let lε:=Sε2​n−1∩Im⁡fl_{\varepsilon}:=S_{\varepsilon}^{2n-1}\cap\operatorname{Im}f be the link of the image of the representative ff. Then it is clear that lεl_{\varepsilon} is homeomorphic to LεL_{\varepsilon} for ε<ε0\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}.

Moreover, since we are working with germ we can choose our representatives such that each irreducible component Ci⊂Σ⁡(f)C_{i}\subset\Sigma(f) is homeomorphic to a cone over its link KiK_{i}, which is a knot in lεl_{\varepsilon}. We can also choose the representative so small, such that Σ⁡(f)\Sigma(f) intersects Sε2​n−1S^{2n-1}_{\varepsilon} transversely for ε<ε0\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0}. Then the conical structure theorem implies that Xε0∖Σ⁡(f)X_{\varepsilon_{0}}\setminus\Sigma(f) is homeomorphic to L^×(0,ε0)\hat{L}\times(0,\varepsilon_{0}), where L^=lε∖⋃i=1kKi\hat{L}=l_{\varepsilon}\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}K_{i}. This is of course only true if 00 is a critical value, but if 00 is not a critical value then ff is an embedding and the result is trivial.

This implies that f|f−1​(Xε0∖Σ⁡(f)):f−1​(Xε0∖Σ⁡(f))→L^×(0,ε0)f|_{f^{-1}\bigl(X_{\varepsilon_{0}}\setminus\Sigma(f)\bigr)}:f^{-1}\bigl(X_{\varepsilon_{0}}\setminus\Sigma(f)\bigr)\to\hat{L}\times(0,\varepsilon_{0}) is a covering map. So f−1​(Xε0∖Σ⁡(f))f^{-1}\bigl(X_{\varepsilon_{0}}\setminus\Sigma(f)\bigr) is homeomorphic to L~×(0,ε0)\widetilde{L}\times(0,\varepsilon_{0}) where L~\widetilde{L} is a finite cover of L^\hat{L}.

Now L^\hat{L} is a graph manifold with a finite number of knots removed, and by the transversality of Σ⁡(f)\Sigma(f) and Sε2​n−1S^{2n-1}_{\varepsilon} we have that these knots are fibres of Seifert fibred pieces of L^\hat{L}. Since L~\widetilde{L} is a finite cover of L^\hat{L} we also have that it is a graph manifold with a finite number of fibres removed from its Seifert fibred pieces.

Let DiD_{i} be a conical neighbourhood of Ci∖{0}C_{i}\setminus\{0\}. That is DiD_{i} is homeomorphic to a tubular neighbourhood of the image of Ci∖{0}C_{i}\setminus\{0\} under the homeomorphism Xε0∖{0}≈lε×(0,ε0)X_{\varepsilon_{0}}\setminus\{0\}\approx l_{\varepsilon}\times(0,\varepsilon_{0}) and Di∩Dj=∅D_{i}\cap D_{j}=\emptyset if i≠ji\neq j.

Topological DiD_{i} is just a cylinder times a disc with the central cylinder being the set of critical values. We can also choose DiD_{i} such that Di∩Sε2​n−1D_{i}\cap S^{2n-1}_{\varepsilon} is a solid torus neighbourhood homeomorphic to a neighbourhood TiT_{i} of the singular fibre KiK_{i} in a Seifert fibred piece of lεl_{\varepsilon}, one of the fibres removed in L^\hat{L}. This means that f|f−1​(Di):f−1​(Di)→Dif|_{f^{-1}\bigl(D_{i}\bigr)}:f^{-1}\bigl(D_{i}\bigr)\to D_{i} is a branched cover branched along the central cylinder. So we get that its connected components are also cylinders times disks, and in particular that f−1​(Ti)f^{-1}\bigl(T_{i}\bigr) is a union of solid tori neighbourhoods of the components of f−1​(Ki)f^{-1}\bigl(K_{i}\bigr).

Since the fibrations f|L~f|_{\widetilde{L}} and f|f−1​(Ti)f|_{f^{-1}(T_{i})} comes from the restrictions they agree on L~∩f−1​(Ti)\widetilde{L}\cap f^{-1}(T_{i}) for each ii. Hence we get that S~=f−1​(L)=L~∪⋃i=1kf−1​(Ti)\widetilde{S}=f^{-1}(L)=\widetilde{L}\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}f^{-1}(T_{i}) is a graph manifold. Technically the structure we get by the gluing might just be the structure of a graph orbifold (see [Ped11]), but every graph orbifold have an underlying space that is a graph manifold, so the topological argument that follows is not a problem.

These considerations implies that f−1​(Xε0∖{0})f^{-1}(X_{\varepsilon_{0}}\setminus\{0\}) is homeomorphic to S~×(0,ε0)\widetilde{S}\times(0,\varepsilon_{0}). Now choosing a closed ball B¯δ⊂Bε0\overline{B}_{\delta}\subset B_{\varepsilon_{0}}, then f−1​((B¯δ∩Im⁡(F))∖{0})f^{-1}\bigl((\overline{B}_{\delta}\cap\operatorname{Im}(F))\setminus\{0\}\bigr) is homeomorphic to S~×(0,δ]\widetilde{S}\times(0,\delta]. Since we have chosen ff proper and f−1​(0)={0}f^{-1}(0)=\{0\} it follows that f−1​(B¯δ∩Im⁡(f))f^{-1}(\overline{B}_{\delta}\cap\operatorname{Im}(f)) is the cone over S~\widetilde{S}. Since f−1​(B¯δ∩Im⁡(F))∖S~f^{-1}(\overline{B}_{\delta}\cap\operatorname{Im}(F))\setminus\widetilde{S} is an open subset of ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2} the result follows from Lemma 3.1

∎

Here we constructed the cone structure on the preimage by topological methods specific to three dimensional manifolds. To prove this theorem in any dimension the best way would probably follow what Fukuda did and construct vector fields that can be integrated to give the cone structure.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.
(II) ⇒\Rightarrow (I)

First (II) implies that we have the quotient map Q:(ℂ2,0)→(X,0)Q:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(X,0) and since the group is finite, this is a finite map. If i:(X,0)→(ℂn,0)i:(X,0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) for some nn is an embedding, then F=i∘QF=i\circ Q is the germ of a finite holomorphic map (ℂ2,0)→(ℂn,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) with (X,0)(X,0) as its image.

(I) ⇒\Rightarrow (III)

Assume that (X,0)⊂(ℂn,0)(X,0)\subset(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) is the image of the germ of a finite map F:(ℂ2,0)→(ℂn,0)F:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0).

Let LL be the link of (X,0)(X,0) chosen as in Lemma 3.2. Hence we have a surjective map f:S3→Lf\colon S^{3}\to L gotten by restricting a representative of FF to S~\widetilde{S} and identifying S~\widetilde{S} with S3S^{3}. Since (X,0)(X,0) is normal, then LL is an oriented graph manifold. Hence we start our analysis just considering maps from S3S^{3} to oriented graph manifolds with a negative definite plumbing.

Let us consider two cases. The first is the case where π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is infinite. Let L~\widetilde{L} be the universal cover of LL, then πi​(L~)=πi​(L)\pi_{i}(\widetilde{L})=\pi_{i}(L) for i>1i>1 and π1​(L~)={0}\pi_{1}(\widetilde{L})=\{0\}. By Corollary 2.3 π2​(L)={0}\pi_{2}(L)=\{0\} since LL is irreducible. Then by the Hurewicz Theorem it follows that π3​(L)=π3​(L~)=H3​(L~)\pi_{3}(L)=\pi_{3}(\widetilde{L})=H_{3}(\widetilde{L}), and H3​(L~)={0}H_{3}(\widetilde{L})=\{0\} since L~\widetilde{L} is non compact because π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is infinite. Notice that continuing this by induction we can prove that LL is an Eilenberg-MacLane space K⁡(π1,1)K(\pi_{1},1).

Since π3​(L)={0}\pi_{3}(L)=\{0\} we have that ff is homotopic to a constant map since it is a map from S3S^{3} to LL. Because the topological degree is a homotopy invariant it follows that degt⁡(f)=0\deg_{t}(f)=0.

Let 0<ε′<ε0<\varepsilon^{\prime}<\varepsilon then f′:F−1​(Sε′2​n−1)→Sε′3f^{\prime}\colon F^{-1}(S_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}^{2n-1})\to S_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}^{3} by the above arguments is also a map from a sphere to a link of (X,0)(X,0) and hence degt⁡(f′)=0\deg_{t}(f^{\prime})=0. Let A⊂ℂnA\subset\mathbbm{C}^{n} be the annulus bound by Sε2​n−1S_{\varepsilon}^{2n-1} and Sε′2​n−1S_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}^{2n-1} and M:=F−1​(A)∈ℂ2M:=F^{-1}(A)\in\mathbbm{C}^{2}. Notice that MM is the region in ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2} bound by F−1​(Sε2​n−1)F^{-1}(S_{\varepsilon}^{2n-1}) and F−1​(Sε′2​n−1)F^{-1}(S_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}^{2n-1}), and therefore a compact manifold with boundary whose interior is a complex manifold. (The boundary might have corneres, but they can canonically be smooted with out changing any topology and only modifying small neighbourhoods of the corners.)

Consider F′:=F|M:M→A∩XF^{\prime}:=F|_{M}\colon M\to A\cap X. Notice that A∩XA\cap X is a complex manifold with boundaries, since XX is normal and hence has an isolated singularity, so we can choose our ε\varepsilon such that Bε∩(X∖{0})B_{\varepsilon}\cap(X\setminus\{0\}) is a complex manifold. F′F^{\prime} is a smooth map, holomorphic on the interior of MM, and degt⁡F′=degt⁡F′|∂M=degt⁡f=degt⁡f′=0\deg_{t}F^{\prime}=\deg_{t}F^{\prime}|_{\partial M}=\deg_{t}f=\deg_{t}f^{\prime}=0 by the above consideration and 13.2.1 Theorem of [DFN85]. Since F′F^{\prime} is smooth, then one can calculate its topological degree as the sums of the signs of the Jacobian determinants at the preimages of a regular value in the interior of AA. But F′F^{\prime} is holomorphic in the interior and hence the sign of the Jacobian determinants are always positive. So degt⁡F′=0\deg_{t}F^{\prime}=0 implies that the preimage of a regular value is empty. This is absurd since F′F^{\prime} is surjective by construction, and the set of critical values have measure 00 in AA by Sard’s Theorem.

So only the case where π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is finite can happen, and we have proved (III).

(III) ⇒\Rightarrow (II)

By Prill’s Theorem 3 [Pri67] it follows that the image of FF is a quotient of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) by a group of biholomorphisms of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) isomorphic to π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L). Since LL is the link of a of a singularity it is a graph manifold, and by Proposition 2.6 any incompressible tori would give an ℤ2\mathbbm{Z}^{2} summand of π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L). So LL can only have a single componenet in its JSJ-decomposition since π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is finite, and hence LL is Seifert fibred. It then follows form the work of Seifert [Sei33] and Hopf [Hop26] that π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is a a subgroup of U⁡(2)U(2) acting linearly.

We could instead refer to Brieskorn’s classification of normal surface singularities with finite fundamental group [Bri68] for this direction. ∎

As we saw in the proof the link of the image LL is a quotient of S3S^{3} by a finite subgroup of S​O​(4)SO(4) acting linearly. This implies that they are Seifert fibred. The topology of these manifolds and therefore their fundamental groups are well know. They were first classified by Hopf [Hop26] and Seifert [Sei33], see also Scott [Sco83] and Orlik [Orl72] for presentation of this. In [Bri68] Brieskorn also derives these results while classifying singularities with finite fundamental group using more algebraic methods.

The topological types comes in several infinite classes which we will discuss individually in more detail in the Section 5. One thing to be aware of is that not all the actions of the subgroups of S​O​(4)SO(4) give actions on ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2}, so some topologies presented in [Sco83] and [Orl72] the are not singularity links. We will of course explain which are singularity links, but even in these case it might be possible that some action of their fundamental group, different from the ones we will present later, does not act on ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2}.

In all cases it will follow that the singularities are rational from using Laufer’s criteria [Lau72] on the minimal dual resolution graphs we present in the section 5. In particular the answer to Peñafort’s original question is; only the simple singularities AnA_{n}, DnD_{n}, E6E_{6}, E7E_{7} and E8E_{8} can be image of a germ of a finite map from (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) to (ℂ3,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{3},0), since these are the only hypersurface singularities that are rational.

The dual resolution graphs will also show using the work of Laufer [Lau73] that all these singularities are taut, that is each topology supports a unique algebraic structure. So we will in Section 5 focus on the topological properties.

4. The Non Normal Case

Example 4.1.

Consider the singularity (X,0)⊂ℂ3(X,0)\subset\mathbbm{C}^{3} given by x​yn−q+zn=0xy^{n-q}+z^{n}=0 with gcd⁡(n,q)=1\gcd(n,q)=1. Then F⁡(s,t)=(sn,tq,s​t)F(s,t)=(s^{n},t^{q},st) is a parametrization of (X,0)(X,0). But if q≠n−1q\neq n-1 then (X,0)(X,0) is not a simple singularity, it is easy to see since its multiplicity is not 22. This does not contradict the conclusion of the last Section, since (X,0)(X,0) is not normal. In fact it does not have an isolated singularity, since the xx-axis is the singular set.

If F:(ℂ2,0)→(X,0)F:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(X,0) is a finite holomorphic map, then by the universal property of normalization, since ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2} is normal, there exist a commutative diagram

where G:(X~,0)→(X,0)G\colon(\widetilde{X},0)\to(X,0) is the normalization. Because FF is finite it is clear that F~\widetilde{F} is also finite and since F−1​(0)={0}F^{-1}(0)=\{0\} the same is true for F~\widetilde{F}. We can then use Section 5 to conclude that (X~,0)(\widetilde{X},0) is one of the singularities described there.

If (X,0)⊂(ℂ3,0)(X,0)\subset(\mathbbm{C}^{3},0) then (X~,0)(\widetilde{X},0) wont necessarily be a hypersurface, and in Example 4.1 the normalization is a cyclic quotient singularity with link the lens space L⁡(n,q)L(n,q), which is not a hypersurface unless q=n−1q=n-1.

If (X,0)⊂(ℂn,0)(X,0)\subset(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) is locally irreducible then the normalization map G:(X~,0)→(X,0)G\colon(\widetilde{X},0)\to(X,0) is a homeomorphism see Section 12.2.6 of [N2́2]. In this case the topologies described in Section 5 are also the possible topologies of (X,0)(X,0). But be aware that links might not be smoothly embedded in ℂn\mathbbm{C}^{n}. In particular, if n=3n=3 then (X,0)(X,0) not being normal is the same as having non isolated singularities. So normalizations are only needed in this case if the singularities are non isolated as in Example 4.1.

If (X,0)(X,0) is not locally irreducible, then we can have singularities like the Whitney umbrella x2−y2​z=0x^{2}-y^{2}z=0 which is the image of (s​t,s,t2)(st,s,t^{2}). Notice that the map is generically one to one, so the map restricted to S3S^{3} is also generically one to one and hence the normalization is smooth. But the link is not S3S^{3} since it has double points.

To conclude. If one have a singularity (X,0)⊂(ℂn,0)(X,0)\subset(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0) and want to see if it is the image of a finite map, then the first step is to normalize (X,0)(X,0). The second step is to identify if (X~,0)(\widetilde{X},0) is a quotient singularity, which can be done by looking at the topology of the link. To construct a map with (X,0)(X,0) as the image, one needs to construct a map to (X~,0)(\widetilde{X},0), which can be done using the quotient construction as seen in Section 5, and then compose with the normalization map. Which is exactly the procedure of Algorithm 1.2

5. Topology, Action and Maps

In this section we will do two things, first give a complete description of the topologies that can appear as the image of a germ of a finite map. This will be done by describing the Seifert invariants of the link, givening the plumbing diagram of the link/dual resolution graph of the singularity, and finally describing the fundamental group of the link. Notice as mentioned in the end of the Section 3, this topological description also completely determines the algebraic structure of the images, since these singularities are taut.

The second thing we do in this section is to give the procedure for how given one of the topologies one can find equations that give a singularity with the given topology and a map from ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2} to ℂn\mathbbm{C}^{n} that have this singularity as its image. We will completely do the cases of the simple singularities, which are the cases n=3n=3 and do some examples with higher embedding dimension.

It follows form the classification of Siefert fibred manifolds that we can divide the ones with finite fundamental group in two different classes. The first class is the Lens spaces L⁡(p,q)L(p,q) that have fundamental group a cyclic group ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/p\mathbbm{Z}, and corresponds to to the cyclic quotient singularities. These manifolds do not have unique Seifert fibred structure.

The the manifolds in the other class have a unique Seifert fibred structure and is fibred over the sphere with at least 3 singular fibres. Form Table 4.1 on page 441 of [Sco83] we have that these topologies are determined by the following inequalities concerning the orbifold Euler characteristic χ⁡(L)\chi(L) and the rational Euler number e⁡(L)e(L):

χ⁡(L)>0\displaystyle\chi(L)>0 and e⁡(L)≠0.\displaystyle e(L)\neq 0.

We will for convenience follow the conventions of [Neu07] for the normalized Seifert invariants {0,(1,−b)​(p1,q1),…,(pk,qk)}\{0,(1,-b)(p_{1},q_{1}),\dots,(p_{k},q_{k})\} of LL. Then the rational euler number and the orbifold euler characteristic are given by the formulas:

χ⁡(L)=2−k+∑i=1k1pi\displaystyle\chi(L)=2-k+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{p_{i}} and e⁡(L)=−b+∑i=1kqipi.\displaystyle e(L)=-b+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{q_{i}}{p_{i}}.

From the first inequality it follows that there are only 33 singular fibres and the Seifert invariants have to be on the form {(1,−b)​(2,1)​(2,1)​(p,q)}\{(1,-b)(2,1)(2,1)(p,q)\}, {(1,−b)​(2,1)​(3,q1)​(3,q2)}\{(1,-b)(2,1)(3,q_{1})(3,q_{2})\}, {(1,−b)​(2,1)​(3,q1)​(4,q2)}\{(1,-b)(2,1)(3,q_{1})(4,q_{2})\} or {(1,−b)​(2,1)​(3,q1)​(5,q2)}\{(1,-b)(2,1)(3,q_{1})(5,q_{2})\}. Since LL is the link of a singularity the plumbing has to be negative definite, but that is the same as e⁡(L)<0e(L)<0 which can bee seen from the description below. So using the second equation one gets that b>1b>1.

As mentioned earlier graph manifolds also have a description as plumbed 3-manifolds, which we will briefly describe. Let E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} be two disc bundles over compact surfaces Σ1\Sigma_{1} and Σ2\Sigma_{2} respectively and let eie_{i} be the euler number of the bundle EiE_{i}. If Σi\Sigma_{i} is orientable then EiE_{i} can be seen as the unit disc bundle in a complex line LiL_{i} bundle and ei=c1​(Li)e_{i}=c_{1}(L_{i}) is the first Chern class of this bundle. Let D~i⊂Σi\widetilde{D}_{i}\subset\Sigma_{i} be a disc such that EiE_{i} trivializes over it. We have subsets D1×D~1⊂E1D_{1}\times\widetilde{D}_{1}\subset E_{1} and D2×D~2⊂E2D_{2}\times\widetilde{D}_{2}\subset E_{2}, and by identifying all discs with the standard dice we can define a gluing of E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} by φ:D1×D~1→D2×D~2\varphi\colon D_{1}\times\widetilde{D}_{1}\to D_{2}\times\widetilde{D}_{2} where φ⁡(x,y)=(y,x)\varphi(x,y)=(y,x). That is we identify the fibres in one fibration with the disc in the base of the other fibration.

If one have a finite collection of disc bundles E1E_{1},…,EkE_{k}, then one can continue to do this process provided that we never glue along subsets that have already been used for the gluing once before. The result is a plumbed four manifold, and we can store the data of the construction in a plumbing graph which have a vertex viv_{i} for each EiE_{i} an edge between viv_{i} and vjv_{j} if the corresponding disc bundles are glued. We decorate the vertices of the graph with the euler number of the corresponding disc bundle and genus of the base surface of the fibration (usually we do not write the genus if it is 00). Then the plumbing graph give a way to construct the plumbed four manifold which is unique up to homeomorphism.

A plumbed 3-manifold is the boundary of a plumbed four manifold after smoothing the corners. A plumbing graph of a plumbed four manifold is also a plumbing graph of its 3-manifold boundary. But in this case it is not unique, there exist a series of plumbing moves that can be used to change the plumbed four manifold without changing its boundary. But Neumann proves in [Neu81] that there exist a unique normal form plumbing diagram. Which in our case can be described as any vertex viv_{i} with only one or two neighbors and a genus weight of 00 have euler number ei≤−2e_{i}\leq-2.

Siefert fibred manifolds are plumbed manifolds, their plumbing graphs are star shaped with a central vertex that can have a base with genus different from 00 and with one leg (or bamboo) for each singular fibre, along which all the base surfaces are spheres. If the Seifert invariants are {g,(1,−b)​(p1,q1),…,(pk,qk)}\{g,(1,-b)(p_{1},q_{1}),\dots,(p_{k},q_{k})\} then the plumbing graph is:

Notice that since ei​j≤−2e_{ij}\leq-2 they are uniquely determined by p1/qip_{1}/q_{i}. For this construction see Section 5 of [Neu81] but be aware that Neumann there uses a different convention for the Seifert invariants, so the formulas are a little different in the one we use.

Below we list the different minimal plumbing graphs for the given Seifert invariants, which in the case of lens spaces is just the numbers (p,q)(p,q). Afterwards we run Laufer’s algorithm [Lau72] to calculate the minimal cycle Zm​i​nZ_{min}. The algorithm will in all cases show that (X,0)(X,0) is a rational singularity and hence Zm​i​n=Zm​a​xZ_{min}=Z_{max} the maximal ideal cycle. Since the multiplicity of (X,0)(X,0) is equal to −Zm​a​x2-Z_{max}^{2} we calculate its value from the Seifert invariants. This is later useful, since (X,0)(X,0) being rational implies that Abyankar’s inequality is a equality, and therefore that the minimal embedding dimension is equal to mult⁡(X,0)+1\operatorname{mult}(X,0)+1. We also describe which group acts in each case.

To construct actual maps with a given singularity (X,0)(X,0) as its image, we will construct (X,0)(X,0) as the the quotients of a given action on (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) obtaining the quotient maps in the process. To construct a geometric quotient of an action by and algebraic group GG on (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) one can do it in the following way using the geometric invariant theory of Mumford [Mum65]: The local algebra of the quotient is ℂ[u,v,]G\mathbbm{C}[u,v,]^{G} the ring of invariants of the action. To find this ring we first find a generating set of invariant polynomials p1p_{1}, p2,p_{2},…, pkp_{k}. Here we can use that we first found the embedding dimension, so once we have as many algebraically independent polynomials as the embedding dimension we can stop looking for more. Then ℂ​[u,v]G≅ℂ⁡[x1,…,xk]/I\mathbbm{C}[u,v]^{G}\cong\mathbbm{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{k}]/I where II is the ideal generated by all the relations arising form setting xi=pi​(u,v)x_{i}=p_{i}(u,v). Here we unfortunately do not have an upper bound of the number of algebraically independent relations except it is higher than k−2k-2 unless the quotient is a simple singularity. But II is the kernal of a map and hence using computer algebra we can find a minimal set of generators as we will see later. The map F:(ℂ2,0)→(ℂk,0)F:(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0)\to(\mathbbm{C}^{k},0) with image the given singularity is then F⁡(u,v)=(p1​(u,v),p2​(u,v),…,pk​(u,v))F(u,v)=\bigl(p_{1}(u,v),p_{2}(u,v),\dots,p_{k}(u,v)\bigr).

5.1. Cyclic Quotients

The first family of links is the lens spaces L⁡(p,q)L(p,q) with gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1. In this case π1​(L⁡(p,q))=ℤ/p​ℤ\pi_{1}\bigl(L(p,q)\bigr)=\mathbbm{Z}/p\mathbbm{Z} and it acts on S3⊂ℂ2S^{3}\subset\mathbbm{C}^{2} by multiplication with the matrix (e2​π​i/p00e2​π​i​q/p)\begin{pmatrix}e^{2\pi i/p}&0\\ 0&e^{2\pi iq/p}\end{pmatrix}. This action clearly extends over all of ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2} and the image of FF is the cyclic quotient singularity given by this action. Notice here that ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/p\mathbbm{Z} may have many different actions giving possibly different quotients, but non of these are singularity links unless they are diffeomorphic to one of the form above. We will call this action a (p,q)(p,q) action and remember that if q​q′≡1modpqq^{\prime}\equiv 1\mod p then the (p,q)(p,q) and (p,q′)(p,q^{\prime}) actions give homeomorphic and hence isomorphic quotients since as we mentioned before the singularities are taut.

5.2. Binary Polyhedral Quotiones

As we will see below, if π1​(L)\pi_{1}(L) is not a cyclic group it is of the form ℤ/m​ℤ×G\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z}\times G where GG is one of the binary polyhedral groups (binary dihedral groups D4​n∗D_{4n}^{*}, binary tetrahedral group T∗T^{*}, binary octahedral group O∗O^{*}, binary icosahedral group I∗I^{*}) or the groups D2l+2​(2​l+1)′D^{\prime}_{2^{l+2}(2l+1)} or T8⋅3k′T^{\prime}_{8\cdot 3^{k}}. As an aside the binary cyclic groups, that is the double cover of ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/p\mathbbm{Z}, also acts on ℂ2\mathbbm{C}^{2}. But its action is just the action of multiplication by (eπ​i/p00eπ​i/p)\begin{pmatrix}e^{\pi i/p}&0\\ 0&e^{\pi i/p}\end{pmatrix}, which is one of the actions by ℤ/2​p​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/2p\mathbbm{Z} covered under the cyclic quotients.

We will first briefly give a summery of the topology, multiplicity of the singularity and which group acts from the Seifert invariants in the different families. Then afterwards first find maps when the fundamental group is just a binary polyhedral group that acts, and later give examples of products with the cyclic groups. We will briefly discuss the case of the groups being D2l+2​(2​l+1)′D^{\prime}_{2^{l+2}(2l+1)} or T8⋅3k′T^{\prime}_{8\cdot 3^{k}} last.

Notice that maps we construct restrict to the universal covering maps on the link, but that is not the only possibility for maps in these cases. π3​(L)≅π3​(S3)≅ℤ\pi_{3}(L)\cong\pi_{3}(S^{3})\cong\mathbbm{Z}, and any class in there can potentially be represented by the restriction of a finite map from (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) to (ℂn,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{n},0). But notice that the isomorphism π3​(L)≅π3​(S3)\pi_{3}(L)\cong\pi_{3}(S^{3}) is from the fibration sequence and is hence given by the induced map from the quotient map. So any class can be represented as a composition of a map S3→S3S^{3}\to S^{3} composed with the quotient map. This means that any map S3→LS^{3}\to L is homotopic to a map S3→S3S^{3}\to S^{3} composed with the quotient map.

5.3. Maps in the case of the Binary Polyhedral groups

In this section we find concrete maps to the quotients of (ℂ2,0)(\mathbbm{C}^{2},0) by the binary polyhedral groups acting. To do so we calculate quotients by finding invariant polynomials as described in the beginning of this section. The invariant polynomials of the binary polyhedral groups were originally found by Felix Klein in 1884. Here with the help of Guilhermo Peñfort-Sanchis and Mathematica we have created a set of of generators of the ring of invariant polynomials.

First some words about how to obtain them. Remember that the binary groups are the preimages of the polyhedral groups under a double cover S3→S​O​(3)S^{3}\to SO(3). This is not a topological cover, but a lie group cover. Now the lie groups structure on S3S^{3} is usually considered as the group spin 11, but one can also consider it as the groups of unit quaternions. The unit quaternions are isomorphic to S​U​(2)SU(2) where the generators or the quaternions are represented by (1001)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}, (i00−i)\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\ 0&-i\end{pmatrix}, (01−10)\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix} (0ii0)\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix} So the action of the binary polyhedral groups we will use is in this embedding in S​U​(2)SU(2).

The binary dihedral group D4​n∗D_{4n}^{*} can be generated by (eπ​i/n00e−πi/n)\begin{pmatrix}e^{\pi i/n}&0\\ 0&e^{-\pi i/n}\end{pmatrix} and (01−10)\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}. The first generator transforms uu to eπ​i/n​ue^{\pi i/n}u and vv to e−πi/nve^{-\pi i/n}v and the second transforms uu to −v-v and vv to uu. This means that the monomial u​vuv is invariant under the action of the first generator, but transformed into −u​v-uv by the second. Hence pD​1=(u​v)2p_{D1}=(uv)^{2} is invariant under both generators and thus under the whole group. Now u2​nu^{2n} and v2​nv^{2n} are invariant under the first generator but interchanged by the second. So pD​2=u2​n+v2​np_{D2}=u^{2n}+v^{2n} is invariant under the whole group. This also means that u2​n−v2​nu^{2n}-v^{2n} is invariant under the first generator but changes sign under the second, so pD​3=u​v​(u2​n−v2​n)p_{D3}=uv(u^{2n}-v^{2n}) is invariant.

We have now found 33 different invariant polynomials, and it is not hard to see that they are algebraically independent. So we have a generating set of the ring of invariants. If we let x=(u​v)2x=(uv)^{2}, y=u2​n+v2​ny=u^{2n}+v^{2n} and z=u​v​(u2​n−v2​n)z=uv(u^{2n}-v^{2n}) then we get the relation z2=(u​v)2​(u4​n+v4​n−2​(u​v)2​n)=x⁡(y2−4​xn)z^{2}=(uv)^{2}(u^{4n}+v^{4n}-2(uv)^{2n})=x(y^{2}-4x^{n}). Since we know that the quotient is a hypersurface singularity and this is an irreducible polynomial, this is an equation for the image given by the map (u,v)↦((u​v)2,u2​n+v2​n,u​v​(u2​n−v2​n))(u,v)\mapsto\bigl((uv)^{2},u^{2n}+v^{2n},uv(u^{2n}-v^{2n})\bigr).

The cases of T∗T^{*}, O∗O^{*} and I∗I^{*} is similar. The generators as a subgroup of S​U​(2)SU(2) are

T∗\displaystyle T^{*} 12​(1+i1+i−1+i1+i),12​(1+i1−i−1−i1−i)\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+i&1+i\\ -1+i&1+i\end{pmatrix},\ \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+i&1-i\\ -1-i&1-i\end{pmatrix}
O∗\displaystyle O^{*} 12​(1+i1+i−1+i1+i),12​(01+i−1+i0)\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+i&1+i\\ -1+i&1+i\end{pmatrix},\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}0&1+i\\ -1+i&0\end{pmatrix}
I∗\displaystyle I^{*} 12​(1+i1+i−1+i1+i),12​(21+5+i​1+521−121+5+i​1+52)\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+i&1+i\\ -1+i&1+i\end{pmatrix},\ \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{2}{1+\sqrt{5}}+i\tfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}&1\\ -1&\tfrac{2}{1+\sqrt{5}}+i\tfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\end{pmatrix}

It is not difficult to see that these matrices satisfies the relations of the generators of their respective groups. To find the invariant polynomials we do the same process as in the binary dihedral case. Testing polynomials until we have three algebraically independent invariant polynomials. In this case the calculations becomes increasingly harder and we used the computer algebra system Matematica to aid us. In the later case even if we made assumption about the polynomials being symmetric or antisymmetric Matematica had problems solving them, and we had to simplify the expression by using partial solutions to get the program to give a solution.

This gave us the following list of invariant polynomials:

5.4. Maps for the product of Cyclic and Binary polyhedral groups

Consider the case of the fundamental group being ℤ/m​ℤ×G\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z}\times G where GG is a binary polyhedral group and m>1m>1. In this case we cannot find the groups acting as subgroups of S​U​(2)SU(2), since the only finite subgroups of S​U​(2)SU(2) are the binary polyhedral groups. Instead we will find them acting as subgroups of of U⁡(2)U(2). If A,BA,B are subgroups of some group CC, then the set A​B={a​b∈C|a∈A​ and ​b∈B}AB=\{ab\in C\,|\,a\in A\text{ and }b\in B\} is a subgroups if either AA or BB is normal in CC. If furthermore A∩B={id}A\cap B=\{\operatorname{id}\} and both AA and BB are normal in A​BAB, then A​BAB is isomorphic to A×BA\times B.

Let G⊂S​U​(2)⊂U⁡(2)G\subset SU(2)\subset U(2) be one of the binary polyhedral groups considered above, and consider ℤ/m​ℤ⊂U⁡(2)\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z}\subset U(2) as the subgroup generated by (e2​π​i/m00e2​π​i/m)\begin{pmatrix}e^{2\pi i/m}&0\\ 0&e^{2\pi i/m}\end{pmatrix}. Then ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} is in the center of U⁡(2)U(2) and hence normal so (ℤ/m​ℤ)​G(\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z})G is a subgroup of U⁡(2)U(2). ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} is still in the center of (ℤ/m​ℤ)​G(\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z})G so it follows that ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} is normal in (ℤ/m​ℤ)​G(\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z})G. Since every element in (ℤ/m​ℤ)​G(\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z})G consist of products of elements that are in GG or commutes with GG it follows that GG is also normal in (ℤ/m​ℤ)​G(\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z})G. Lastly, since elements in ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} has order a divisor of mm, and by construction mm is coprime with the order of GG we have that (ℤ/m​ℤ)∩G={id}(\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z})\cap G=\{\operatorname{id}\}. So we get that the group generated by (e2​π​i/m00e2​π​i/m)\begin{pmatrix}e^{2\pi i/m}&0\\ 0&e^{2\pi i/m}\end{pmatrix} and the generators of GG is the fundamental group of the link.

To find the invariant polynomials we just have to intersect the invariant polynomials we found for the given binary polyhedral group with the invariant polynomials for the given action of ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z}. In 5.1.1 we found this to be generated by all monomials on the form ua​vbu^{a}v^{b} where a+b=ma+b=m. Notice that in this case the action is simply given by multiplying each variable by a mm root of unity ξm\xi_{m}. This implies that the action will transform any monomial of degree dd by multiplying with ξmd\xi_{m}^{d}. It will then of course also transform a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd by multiplying it with ξmd\xi_{m}^{d}. So any homogeneous polynomial is invariant under the action of ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} if and only if it have degree a multiple of mm. Furthermore any invariant polynomial will have that any of its homogeneous components are invariant under the action, and in particular any monomial in an invariant polynomial have degree a multiple of mm.

Let p∗1p_{*1}, p∗2p_{*2} and p∗3p_{*3} be the generators of the invariant polynomials under the action of the give binary polyhedral group. Let d∗id_{*i} be the degree of p∗ip_{*i}, then because p∗ip_{*i} is homogenous the action of the generator of ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} will just be multiplication by ξmd∗i\xi_{m}^{d_{*i}}. An invariant polynomial of the form p∗1a1​p∗2a2​p∗3a3p_{*1}^{a_{1}}p_{*2}^{a_{2}}p_{*3}^{a_{3}} will be transformed into ξma1​d∗1+a2​d∗2+a3​d∗3​p∗1a1​p∗2a2​p∗3a3\xi_{m}^{a_{1}d_{*1}+a_{2}d_{*2}+a_{3}d_{*3}}p_{*1}^{a_{1}}p_{*2}^{a_{2}}p_{*3}^{a_{3}}, and hence be invariant if and only if a1​d∗1+a2​d∗2+a3​d∗3a_{1}d_{*1}+a_{2}d_{*2}+a_{3}d_{*3} is a multiple of mm. When we want to find generator we can furthermore assume that m2m^{2} does not divide a1​d∗1+a2​d∗2+a3​d∗3a_{1}d_{*1}+a_{2}d_{*2}+a_{3}d_{*3}. Since any invariant polynomial under the action of the binary polyhedral group must be a polynomial in d∗1d_{*1}, d∗2d_{*2} and d∗3d_{*3} we get that the invariant polynomials under the product group is generated by monomial of the form p∗1a1​p∗2a2​p∗3a3p_{*1}^{a_{1}}p_{*2}^{a_{2}}p_{*3}^{a_{3}} with a1​d∗1+a2​d∗2+a3​d∗3a_{1}d_{*1}+a_{2}d_{*2}+a_{3}d_{*3} a multiple of mm.

5.4.1. GG is the Binary Dihedral group

In the case of D4​n∗D_{4n}^{*} the degrees of the generators are dD​1=4d_{D1}=4, dD​2=2​nd_{D2}=2n and dD​3=2​n+1d_{D3}=2n+1 and we have that m=(b−1)​n−qm=(b-1)n-q with gcd⁡(m,2​n)=1\gcd(m,2n)=1 and gcd⁡(n,q)=1\gcd(n,q)=1. So the equation defining the power of the invariant polynomials is 4​a1+2​n​a2+(2​n+2)​a3=l​m=l⁡((b−1)​n−q)4a_{1}+2na_{2}+(2n+2)a_{3}=lm=l\bigl((b-1)n-q\bigr) for some ll. Since mm is odd we can assume that ll is even and replace with l′=l/2l^{\prime}=l/2 and get 2​a1+n​a2+(n+1)​a3=l′​m=l′​((b−1)​n−q)2a_{1}+na_{2}+(n+1)a_{3}=l^{\prime}m=l^{\prime}\bigl((b-1)n-q\bigr). For given values of nn, bb and qq this equation is not hard to solve.

Example 5.3.

Assume that b=3b=3, n=2n=2 and q=1q=1 the equation becomes 2​a1+2​a2+3​a3=3​l′2a_{1}+2a_{2}+3a_{3}=3l^{\prime}. The solutions for (a1,a2,a3)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}) are (3,0,0)(3,0,0), (2,1,0)(2,1,0), (1,2,0)(1,2,0), (0,3,0)(0,3,0) and (0,0,1)(0,0,1), and we get the polynomials (v​v)6(vv)^{6}, (u​v)4​(u4+v4)(uv)^{4}(u^{4}+v^{4}), (u​v)2​(u4+v4)2(uv)^{2}(u^{4}+v^{4})^{2}, (u4+v4)3(u^{4}+v^{4})^{3} and u​v​(u4−v4)uv(u^{4}-v^{4}). But notice that (u​v​(u4−v4))2+4​(u​v)6=(u​v)2​(u8+v8−2​(u​v)4)+4​(u​v)6=(u​v)2​(u8+v8+2​(u​v)4)=(u​v)2​(u4+v4)2(uv(u^{4}-v^{4}))^{2}+4(uv)^{6}=(uv)^{2}(u^{8}+v^{8}-2(uv)^{4})+4(uv)^{6}=(uv)^{2}(u^{8}+v^{8}+2(uv)^{4})=(uv)^{2}(u^{4}+v^{4})^{2}. So we only have the four algebraically independent generators (u​v)6(uv)^{6}, (u​v)4​(u4+v4)(uv)^{4}(u^{4}+v^{4}), (u4+v4)3(u^{4}+v^{4})^{3} and u​v​(u4−v4)uv(u^{4}-v^{4}). The equations can again be found as the kernel of a ring homomorphism which we here have calculated using singular and get the equations of the image y​w2+4​x​y−x​z=0yw^{2}+4xy-xz=0, x​w2+4​x2−y2+0xw^{2}+4x^{2}-y^{2}+0 and w4−16​x2+8​y2−y​z=0w^{4}-16x^{2}+8y^{2}-yz=0, for the map F⁡(u,v)=((u​v)6,(u​v)4​(u4+v4),(u4+v4)3,u​v​(u4−v4))F(u,v)=\bigl((uv)^{6},(uv)^{4}(u^{4}+v^{4}),(u^{4}+v^{4})^{3},uv(u^{4}-v^{4})\bigr).

5.4.2. GG is the Binary Tetrahedral group

In the case of T∗T^{*} the degrees of the generating invariant polynomials are dT​1=6d_{T1}=6, dT​2=8d_{T2}=8 and dT​3=12d_{T3}=12, m=6​b−3−2​q1−2​q2m=6b-3-2q_{1}-2q_{2} and gcd⁡(m,12)=1\gcd(m,12)=1. So the equation defining products of pT​1p_{T1}, pT​2p_{T2} and pT​3p_{T3} being invariant under the action of ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} is 6​a1+8​a2+12​a3=l​m=l⁡(6​b−3−2​q1−2​q2)6a_{1}+8a_{2}+12a_{3}=lm=l\bigl(6b-3-2q_{1}-2q_{2}\bigr). Since mm is always odd we can replace ll by l′=l/2l^{\prime}=l/2 and reduce the equation to 3​a1+4​a2+6​a3=l′​m=l′​(6​b−3−2​q1−2​q2)3a_{1}+4a_{2}+6a_{3}=l^{\prime}m=l^{\prime}\bigl(6b-3-2q_{1}-2q_{2}\bigr). 5.5. The Non Binary polyhedral case

In the case of the group being D2k+2​(2​l+1CLOSE′D^{\prime}_{2^{k+2}(2l+1} or T∗8⋅3kT*_{8\cdot 3^{k}} we cannot find embedding of the group into S​U​(2)SU(2) since the only finite subgroups of S​U​(2)SU(2) are the cyclic groups and the binary polyhedral groups. So the representation of the groups have to be in U⁡(2)U(2). These groups are not very studied in the literature, so we could not find concrete representation already given to work with. So no example will be given, but the process is the same find an embedding of the group into U⁡(2)U(2) and calculate the invariant of this action on ℂ⁡[u,v]\mathbbm{C}[u,v]. Then represent ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbbm{Z}/m\mathbbm{Z} by the diagonal action by (e2​π​i/m00e2​π​i/m)\begin{pmatrix}e^{2\pi i/m}&0\\ 0&e^{2\pi i/m}\end{pmatrix} which will because of the conditions on mm commute with the action of D2k+2​(2​l+1CLOSE′D^{\prime}_{2^{k+2}(2l+1} or T∗8⋅3kT*_{8\cdot 3^{k}} so the invariant of the product action is just the intersection of the invariants of the two actions.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
